Pregnancy

Omicron and COVID-19 during pregnancy: symptoms, protection and care

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hearing that a COVID-19 variant is usually mild can be reassuring, but it does not tell you how an infection will affect your pregnancy. Many people recover without serious illness. Pregnancy still changes the balance of risk, making prevention and prompt advice worthwhile even when the first symptoms resemble a cold. The original Omicron wave belongs to the history of the pandemic. Its early symptom reports and vaccine studies are useful only when their dates and limits are clear. Your care today should depend on how you feel, your pregnancy and health history, and current local recommendations: not on an old description of a supposedly harmless variant.

What the early Omicron reports can tell us

Omicron is a family of SARS-CoV-2 variants, the virus that causes COVID-19. It was designated a variant of concern in late November 2021. Names such as B.1.1.529, BA.1, BA.2 and BA.3 describe that early period; they are not a complete list of the variants circulating now.

A December 2021 CDC report described the first 43 confirmed US Omicron cases. Cough, tiredness and a blocked or runny nose were common. That small, early sample was not a study of symptoms unique to pregnancy and could not establish that everyone would have a mild illness.

Some clinicians initially described more upper-airway symptoms with Omicron than the severe breathlessness they had seen during Delta waves. Those observations did not create a reliable way to identify a variant from symptoms. A person with congestion can still become more unwell, and breathing difficulty needs attention whatever the variant is called.

Symptoms to take seriously during pregnancy

Possible symptoms include fever or chills, cough, a sore throat, nasal congestion or a runny nose, tiredness, muscle or body aches, and headache. Some people notice a new change in taste or smell. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea can also occur. Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing is especially important to assess.

Not everyone has every symptom, and the absence of fever or loss of smell does not rule out COVID-19. Symptoms overlap with influenza and other infections. Testing and clinical assessment can help distinguish them when that information affects treatment.

Pregnancy itself can bring fatigue, nausea or changes in breathing, but a new, worsening or unusual symptom should not automatically be attributed to pregnancy. Tell your maternity team what has changed, when it began and whether you have had a positive test or a recent exposure.

Why pregnancy changes the risk

Pregnancy involves changes in immune function, breathing and circulation. It is inaccurate to describe this as the immune system simply shutting down because the baby has different genes. These adaptations are more complex, and the effect of infection depends on the person as well as the virus.

Compared with otherwise similar people who are not pregnant, pregnant and recently pregnant people have a higher risk of severe COVID-19, including illness needing hospital or intensive care. Infection during pregnancy is also associated with a greater chance of preterm birth and some other pregnancy complications. These are increased risks, not predictions that an individual pregnancy will have a poor outcome.

Having symptoms does not mean you must be admitted to intensive care. Decisions depend on breathing, hydration, other illnesses, pregnancy concerns and the clinical assessment. Conversely, vaccination or a description of the circulating variant as mild should not be used to dismiss deteriorating symptoms.

What the Scottish vaccination study actually found

A Scottish population study published in Nature Medicine in January 2022 examined vaccination and infection through 31 October 2021. Of 104 infection-associated critical-care admissions, 102 (about 98%) were in people classified as unvaccinated when infection was diagnosed. That classification included a first vaccine dose given within the preceding 21 days.

This does not mean that 98% of unvaccinated pregnant people needed critical care. It describes the vaccination status of the critical-care group. The study also predates the Omicron wave, so its figure cannot be used as an Omicron-specific risk estimate or a current vaccine-effectiveness percentage.

The finding supports taking vaccination seriously, while the observational design and historical setting limit what it can prove. It does not establish that a vaccinated person has zero risk of hospital admission, ventilation or death.

Vaccination during pregnancy and breastfeeding

A reasonable concern is whether vaccination could harm the pregnancy or baby. Pregnancy safety studies have been reassuring. For example, a CDC study did not find an increased risk of preterm birth or a baby being small for gestational age after COVID-19 vaccination. Small for gestational age means smaller than expected for the length of the pregnancy; it is not exactly the same measurement as low birthweight.

In its March 2026 guidance, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists continued to recommend updated COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy, after pregnancy, while breastfeeding and when considering pregnancy. This is a named professional recommendation, rather than a claim that every country or organisation uses the same schedule.

Vaccination reduces the risk of serious illness but cannot prevent every infection. The old promise that three doses make serious outcomes almost impossible is too strong. The appropriate product and timing depend on current guidance, previous doses, recent infection, health conditions and individual contraindications. Your clinician or pharmacist can help you check those details.

If a previous reaction or conflicting advice is making the decision difficult, describe that concern directly. Ask about the expected benefits, common side effects, unusual reactions that need help and any reason a particular product would be unsuitable for you. Reassurance should leave room for questions rather than imply that any medical intervention is entirely risk-free.

What to do if you become unwell

Contact your maternity team or usual clinician promptly if you develop possible COVID-19 symptoms or test positive. Tell them you are pregnant or recently pregnant, your gestation if relevant, the first day of symptoms, your medicines and any other health conditions. Early contact matters because some treatments need to begin within a short time after illness starts.

Pregnancy or breastfeeding alone is not a reason to withhold appropriate COVID-19 treatment. A prescriber still needs to choose a suitable medicine, check interactions and consider kidney or liver problems and other circumstances. Do not borrow someone else’s antiviral medicine or decide that treatment is unnecessary solely because you have been vaccinated.

If home care is appropriate, agree how you will monitor symptoms and when to call again. Rest, drink enough to stay hydrated and check any medicine for fever or discomfort with your pregnancy-care team or pharmacist. Call before attending a routine appointment so the service can arrange care while reducing exposure to others. An infection should not mean losing access to necessary maternity care.

When to seek urgent help

Get emergency help for serious trouble breathing, persistent chest pain or pressure, new confusion, inability to stay awake, collapse, or a concerning pale, blue or grey colour of the lips or skin. Use the emergency number where you live. Do not wait for a COVID test, a variant result or a routine callback when these symptoms occur.

Contact maternity care immediately for reduced or stopped movements once you normally feel your baby move, bleeding, leaking fluid, severe abdominal pain or a severe headache with visual changes. A fever of 38°C or above, persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down or other marked deterioration also needs prompt medical advice.

These signs are not specific to COVID-19. They may indicate a pregnancy complication or another illness, and having an infection should not prevent those possibilities from being assessed. If you cannot reach your usual maternity service and the situation seems urgent, use another urgent or emergency route.

Protecting yourself with help from your household

Protection is easier when it is shared. Household members can check their own vaccine recommendations, tell you when they are ill, and help with childcare, meals or shopping while you recover. Their vaccination is one useful layer; it does not guarantee that they cannot bring an infection home.

Cleaner indoor air, avoiding close contact with people who are unwell and a well-fitting mask in crowded indoor or poorly ventilated spaces can reduce exposure. Choose precautions that fit the setting and your health circumstances. A blanket instruction to keep a mask on at every moment outside the home is not a substitute for a practical plan.

Keep your maternity contact details accessible and know where to seek advice outside office hours. The aim is to make useful action easier: prevent exposure where possible, recognise a change in symptoms and get timely care without assuming either that every infection is dangerous or that none can be.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Early Omicron case reports describe a historical sample; they cannot diagnose today’s variant or an individual pregnancy’s risk.

CDC identifies pregnancy and recent pregnancy as risk factors for severe illness and advises against withholding appropriate treatment solely because of pregnancy or lactation.

ACOG’s March 2026 vaccination recommendation should be read alongside current local eligibility and product guidance.

How BeMama can help

Make a short care plan with your maternity team: whom to call, what changes need urgent help and how your household can support you if you become unwell.

When to seek help

This is general education, not an individual treatment or vaccine schedule. Serious breathing symptoms and urgent pregnancy warning signs require immediate assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Cold-like symptoms cannot establish the variant or guarantee a mild course.
  • Pregnancy increases risk, but symptoms alone do not mean intensive care is needed.
  • The Scottish 98% figure describes a historical critical-care group, not the chance that an unvaccinated person will become critically ill.
  • Ask promptly about testing, treatment and vaccination appropriate to your circumstances.
  • Seek urgent help for breathing difficulty or maternity warning signs.

Frequently asked questions

Does Omicron cause a different set of symptoms in pregnancy?

There is no symptom checklist that reliably identifies an Omicron infection specifically in pregnancy. Cough, congestion, fatigue and other COVID-19 symptoms overlap with other infections and with some pregnancy experiences. New or worsening symptoms deserve assessment.

Does every pregnant person with COVID-19 need hospital care?

No. Many recover with advice and home care. Hospital or intensive care depends on the illness and pregnancy assessment, not simply a positive test or the presence of symptoms.

Does the Scottish 98% figure mean a 98% chance of severe illness?

No. It was the proportion of infection-associated critical-care admissions occurring in the study’s unvaccinated group. It was not the proportion of all unvaccinated pregnant people who became critically ill.

Can I still become seriously ill after vaccination?

Yes, although vaccination reduces the risk of serious outcomes. New or worsening symptoms should be assessed regardless of how many doses you have received.

Do COVID-19 vaccines cause premature birth or poor growth?

The pregnancy safety evidence reviewed here is reassuring and did not show an increased risk of preterm or small-for-gestational-age birth. Discuss the appropriate product and any individual contraindications with your clinician; no intervention is described as having no possible side effects.

Should I wait to ask about treatment because I am pregnant?

No. Contact a clinician promptly. Appropriate treatment should not be withheld solely because of pregnancy or breastfeeding, and some options have short treatment windows. A prescriber must check suitability and interactions.

Are the first Omicron subvariant names still a useful guide?

They explain the early pandemic reports, but do not provide current surveillance. You do not need to identify a subvariant before seeking help for concerning symptoms.

How can my family help protect me?

They can follow relevant vaccination advice, avoid close contact when ill, improve indoor ventilation and help you access care. Practical help with everyday tasks also makes resting and monitoring symptoms easier.

Should I assume reduced baby movements are just part of COVID-19?

No. Contact maternity care immediately if movements reduce or stop once you normally feel them. Do not wait for an infection to resolve before seeking assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
